paragraphs: Offline goal-conditioned navigation learns how to reach destinations from previously collected trajectories. Graph-based methods can help with long routes, where errors in estimated values accumulate. However, representing an environment with many keypoints makes planning expensive, and a graph built from old data may become unreliable when new obstacles appear.

Adaptive Quasimetric Mapping addresses both problems using a learned estimate of the time needed to travel between states. This estimate is a quasimetric, allowing travel difficulty to depend on direction. The method selects a sparse collection of representative points through a greedy approximation to a dominating set problem, producing a smaller navigation graph.

During deployment, AQM compares actual traversal times with budgets derived from its learned travel-time estimates. It prunes the graph when these checks indicate problems, enabling zero-shot replanning. Across navigation benchmarks, including a video-game-like setting, it achieves competitive performance with up to 100 times fewer keypoints than prior approaches. The findings support sparse graph representations that can respond to changes encountered during navigation.
icml-2026-adaptive-quasimetric-mapping-p.tldr: AQM builds sparse navigation graphs from offline data and prunes unreliable routes during deployment, achieving competitive results with up to 100 times fewer keypoints.

paragraphs: A vector-quantized variational autoencoder represents images using entries from a finite codebook. Because that codebook must support many different visual patterns, its limited capacity can restrict the richness of the learned representation. ArcVQ-VAE focuses on how the available vectors are arranged and used, seeking to encode more diverse information within the constrained representation space.

The proposed spherical angular-margin prior combines two mechanisms. Ball-Bounded Norm Regularization keeps codebook vectors inside a Euclidean ball whose size changes over time. An ArcCosine Additive Margin Loss encourages latent vectors to be more separated in angle. Together, these mechanisms promote representations that are distinguishable and more uniformly dispersed.

This geometric organization is intended to improve codebook utilization and allow its entries to carry richer information. On standard image reconstruction and generation tasks, the authors report improvements over baseline models in reconstruction accuracy, representation diversity, and generated sample quality. The findings connect better use of a finite codebook with gains in both representing existing images and generating new ones.
icml-2026-arcvq-vae-a-spherical-vector-q.tldr: ArcVQ-VAE organizes discrete image representations using norm constraints and angular separation, improving codebook use and image reconstruction and generation results.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning often evaluates future rewards through Bellman recursions, which express a decision's value using values of later decisions. This paper examines what happens when future rewards receive non-exponential discounts, as can occur in human preferences and survival processes. It argues that the failure of standard recursion in these settings has a structural cause.

The analysis identifies two properties that support the standard formulation: multiplicativity and time homogeneity. Exponential discounting satisfies both, while violating either breaks standard dynamic programming. The proposed Pontryagin-Guided Direct Policy Optimization therefore optimizes policies through a variational framework that does not depend on that recursion.

The framework combines the Pontryagin Maximum Principle with Monte Carlo rollouts. An Adjoint-MC projection enforces pointwise Hamiltonian maximization, connecting simulated trajectories to the optimization condition. On multidimensional benchmarks with hyperbolic and survival-based discounting, the authors report better accuracy and stability in settings where equation-driven solvers and critic-based baselines diverge. These results support a different optimization route for the studied discounting structures.
icml-2026-beyond-the-bellman-recursion-a.tldr: PG-DPO uses Pontryagin-guided policy optimization to handle non-exponential discounting where standard Bellman recursions break down.

paragraphs: On-policy preference learning collects training examples using the policy being updated. This paper explains why that can outperform learning from a fixed collection generated by the initial policy. Its central idea is coverage improvement: with sufficiently large batches, each update enters a region around the target where coverage is uniformly better, making later samples more informative.

The main convergence result applies to contextual bandits with Bradley-Terry preferences and a linear softmax policy class. When batch size exceeds a generalized coverage threshold, on-policy DPO converges exponentially with the number of iterations. Learners restricted to the initial policy's offline samples face a slower minimax rate, producing a separation in total sample requirements.

The authors also introduce a hybrid sampler based on preferential G-optimal design that removes coverage dependence and guarantees convergence in two rounds within the analyzed framework. Additional reward-distillation schemes obtain faster noiseless rates. Experiments support the theoretical direction: the proposed on-policy methods outperform their off-policy counterparts and show stable improvements across iterations.
icml-2026-coverage-improvement-and-fast-.tldr: Under specified modeling and batch-size conditions, on-policy preference updates improve sampling coverage and enable faster convergence than fixed offline data.

paragraphs: A retrieval system's evaluation depends on which questions it is asked. If a query collection misses substantial parts of the underlying document corpus, its aggregate scores can give an incomplete picture of performance. This paper formalizes retrieval evaluation as statistical estimation and shows that evaluation-set construction fundamentally limits the reliability of reported metrics.

The proposed semantic stratification method starts from the structure of the corpus. It organizes documents into an interpretable global space of entity-based clusters, then systematically generates queries for strata that lack coverage. This connects the test questions to identifiable parts of the document collection and provides formal semantic coverage guarantees across retrieval regimes.

Experiments across multiple benchmarks and retrieval methods reveal systematic coverage gaps and structural signals that explain variation in performance. Stratified evaluation produces more stable assessments while making retrieval failures easier to interpret. The contribution is an evaluation framework: it helps users understand which parts of a corpus are represented in testing and where a retriever struggles.
icml-2026-coverage-not-averages-semantic.tldr: Semantic stratification builds retrieval evaluations around corpus coverage, producing more stable scores and clearer explanations of retrieval failures.

paragraphs: Many retrieval systems first select a candidate set and then use a second ranker to order those candidates. Training the first stage from the final reward is difficult because ordinary policy gradients treat the entire selected set as the sampled action. As candidate sets grow, the resulting gradient variance can become too large for practical training.

Credit-assigned policy gradient changes where the learning signal is applied. It uses the probability that a target item appears in any candidate set, marginalizing over the different sets that contain it. This reduces dependence on the particular combination of accompanying items and connects the update more directly to an individual item's contribution.

The theoretical analysis shows a substantial variance reduction while retaining the ability to learn the correct item ordering when the late-stage ranking policy is reasonably aligned. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data use early-stage rankers based on the Plackett-Luce model. They show faster convergence and more stable training, with especially clear benefits for large candidate sets.
icml-2026-credit-assigned-policy-gradien.tldr: CA-PG reduces variance in early-stage retrieval training by assigning credit through item-inclusion probabilities rather than whole candidate-set probabilities.

paragraphs: Dataset distillation compresses training information into synthetic data designed for a learning procedure. Although it has shown practical promise, understanding what these synthetic examples capture remains difficult. This paper develops a theoretical account of how practical gradient-based distillation algorithms extract and encode task-relevant structure.

The analysis studies gradient-based training of two-layer neural networks with width L on nonlinear tasks described by a multi-index model. Within this setting, the authors prove that the distilled data efficiently encode the problem's low-dimensional structure. The important distinction is between the full input dimension d and the intrinsic task dimension r, which describes the smaller structure relevant to learning.

The distilled dataset can reproduce a model with high generalization ability at a required memory complexity of approximately r²d + L, with logarithmic factors suppressed in the stated bound. This makes the compression result explicitly dependent on task structure and network width. The contribution is a theoretical explanation for a specified nonlinear setting, linking gradient-based distillation to the efficient storage of low-dimensional representations.
icml-2026-dataset-distillation-efficient.tldr: For a specified nonlinear task family, the paper proves that gradient-based dataset distillation efficiently stores low-dimensional structure while preserving strong generalization.

paragraphs: Scientific data often contain matrix-valued quantities, including covariances, inertias, and shape tensors. Their transformation rules can be broader than those supported by networks designed around compact symmetry groups or ordinary vector features. Reductive Lie Neurons provide an architecture with exact general-linear equivariance, so its features transform consistently under the supported linear symmetries.

The key construction is a non-degenerate bilinear form that remains invariant under conjugation. It addresses a stability issue for reductive Lie algebras and supports both nonlinear interactions and invariant feature construction. The same architecture can transfer across subgroups without requiring a separate redesign for each symmetry setting.

The authors demonstrate the network on algebraic tasks, Lorentz-equivariant particle physics, drone state estimation with velocity and covariance, Gaussian-splat representations, and a double-pendulum benchmark. Across these evaluations, it matches or outperforms strong equivariant and self-supervised baselines while using substantially fewer parameters and less computation. The results support the architecture as a reusable way to process matrix and Lie-algebraic features efficiently.
icml-2026-equivariant-neural-networks-fo.tldr: Reductive Lie Neurons provide exact general-linear equivariance for matrix-valued features, with strong accuracy and efficiency across several scientific and geometric tasks.

paragraphs: For a continuous treatment, the goal is to estimate how the population's average outcome changes across treatment values. Directly regressing outcomes on treatment can be misleading because treatment assignment depends on other observed characteristics. This confounding makes the observed treatment groups systematically different, creating a distribution-shift problem for estimation.

The paper proposes two stages of kernel ridge regression. First, it models outcomes jointly as a function of treatment and covariates. It then uses that model to create pseudo-outcomes that correct for distribution shift, and fits a second regression to estimate the population-level effect function. Averaging over covariates can produce a simpler function than the original response model, and the estimator adapts to that structure.

The authors establish optimal learning bounds without estimating the conditional treatment density, avoiding a stated bottleneck in existing methods. They also provide a fully data-driven model-selection procedure with provable adaptation to unknown overlap and kernel spectral decay. These results connect the estimator's learning guarantees to properties that need not be supplied in advance.
icml-2026-estimating-continuous-treatmen.tldr: Two-stage kernel ridge regression estimates continuous treatment effects using corrected pseudo-outcomes, with adaptive learning guarantees that avoid conditional treatment-density estimation.

paragraphs: Removing names and other explicit identifiers does not necessarily eliminate the information needed to infer someone's identity. This paper studies how LLM agents combine scattered contextual clues with public evidence to reconnect anonymized records to real people. It examines whether agents lower the expertise and manual effort historically associated with this kind of re-identification.

The evaluation covers classical linkage incidents, a controlled benchmark called InferLink, and open-ended human–AI interaction traces. InferLink varies the kinds of identifying patterns available, the task framing, and the agent's prior knowledge. This lets the authors investigate both explicit attempts to identify someone and identity inference that occurs without such a request.

In the sparsest Netflix Prize setting studied, agents reconstruct 79.2% of identities, compared with 56.0% for a classical matching baseline. They also link people in InferLink without explicit re-identification instructions and resolve anonymized profiles in redacted interaction traces. These findings motivate privacy evaluations that assess identities inferable from available information, alongside information access and disclosure.
icml-2026-from-weak-cues-to-real-identit.tldr: LLM agents can combine weak contextual cues with public evidence to identify anonymized people, sometimes even without an explicit re-identification request.

paragraphs: GEAR is a transfer learning framework that brings knowledge from multiple models into a shared architecture. Its central idea is to connect models through the geometry of their latent spaces—the internal representations they learn from data. This gives the framework a way to relate information learned from diverse sources when addressing a target task.

The approach draws on differential geometry, particularly Riemannian geometry, and aligns a geometric quantity called Ricci curvature across the individual models’ latent spaces. Curvature matching is the mechanism used to build connections among the models. The authors describe the resulting architecture as providing a comprehensive geometric representation across data points, supporting the aggregation of knowledge.

The evaluation covers 23 molecular task pairs. The authors report significant performance gains over existing benchmark models, with improvements of at least 14.4% under random splits and 8.3% under scaffold splits. These are results for the two stated evaluation settings; the abstract does not present them as guarantees for arbitrary transfer learning tasks.

The findings support geometry alignment as a useful approach to combining models in the evaluated molecular tasks. The broader contribution is a framework that makes the geometric structure of learned representations central to knowledge transfer, with the reported gains showing its practical value in those evaluations.
icml-2026-geometric-embedding-alignment-.tldr: GEAR combines knowledge from multiple models by matching latent-space Ricci curvature, reporting performance gains across 23 molecular task pairs.

paragraphs: Domain adaptation tries to preserve predictive performance when training and deployment distributions differ. One strategy minimizes a computable part of an optimal-transport bound on target risk. This paper examines when improving that objective can actually improve target accuracy, given that the full bound also contains an entanglement term that cannot be computed.

The authors introduce gradual-shift and probabilistic-margin assumptions to control that inaccessible term. Under these assumptions, they prove that better optimization of the computable portion can translate into better target accuracies. They then tighten the bound by importance-weighting the source output distribution, producing weighted Wasserstein regularized risk, or W²R², which is often easier to minimize.

The resulting objective is equivalent to an unbalanced optimal-transport problem and approaches a nearest-neighbor alignment strategy in a limit. The paper examines the associated tradeoffs and reports that suitable regularization improves on the state of the art across multiple distribution shifts and models. The experiments also support the relevance of the assumptions used in the analysis.
icml-2026-incorporating-importance-weigh.tldr: Importance-weighted optimal transport yields a more tractable domain-alignment objective, with conditional theoretical support and empirical gains under multiple distribution shifts.

paragraphs: Active feature acquisition asks which additional measurement would most improve a prediction for a particular test instance. The decision must be made sequentially, using what is already known. In practice, training data may themselves contain systematic gaps, and only a small number of labels may be available for the task of interest.

Learning-to-Measure combines uncertainty estimation across unseen tasks with an acquisition agent guided by that uncertainty. The agent maximizes conditional mutual information, selecting features for the information they are expected to provide given the current observations. An autoregressive pre-training approach supports uncertainty estimation and acquisition for tasks with arbitrary missingness.

L2M works directly with retrospectively incomplete datasets and performs new tasks in context, without retraining separately for each one. Across synthetic and real-world tabular benchmarks, it matches or exceeds task-specific baselines, with particular strengths when labels are scarce and missingness is high. The findings support using a shared pre-trained system to guide measurement decisions across different tasks.
icml-2026-learning-to-measure-in-context.tldr: L2M uses in-context uncertainty estimates to choose informative measurements, performing well on tabular tasks with scarce labels and substantial missing data.

paragraphs: Many optimization tasks depend on preferences that are difficult to reduce to a numerical score or a choice between two candidates. A decision maker may express several considerations in ordinary language, along with relevant prior knowledge. LILO brings this richer feedback into Bayesian optimization while retaining a statistical model for choosing what to explore next.

An LLM translates free-form feedback and prior knowledge into structured preference signals. A Gaussian process proxy model incorporates those signals, represents uncertainty, and supports acquisition-driven exploration. The language model handles interpretation, while the Bayesian optimization machinery remains responsible for the search process.

This division is designed to preserve Bayesian optimization's sample efficiency and stability while expanding the ways people can communicate preferences. Across synthetic and real-world benchmarks, LILO consistently outperforms conventional preference-based Bayesian optimization and LLM-only optimizers. Its strongest reported gains occur when feedback is limited, supporting the value of extracting richer guidance from the interactions available.
icml-2026-lilo-bayesian-optimization-wit.tldr: LILO translates natural-language preferences into signals for Bayesian optimization, improving results especially when decision-maker feedback is limited.

paragraphs: Predicting how a scene will evolve can help an online video model maintain continuity over time. But during occlusion or rapid motion, inaccurate predictions can contaminate memory and cause the model to lose an object's identity. This paper attributes that failure to applying predictive dynamics uniformly even when observations are weak and uncertainty is high.

Reliability-Guided Predictive Memory treats memory as an evolving latent process. A state-space world model produces predictive priors, while a reliability-aware fusion policy regulates their influence on perception. During occlusion, the policy suppresses predictions judged unreliable, addressing when predictions should affect memory as well as what those predictions contain.

The authors implement RPM in a SAM2-based model and evaluate visual object tracking. It reduces drift after occlusion and consistently outperforms strong baselines using static memory or unconditional prediction. The mechanism also transfers to video object segmentation across several standard benchmarks. These findings support explicitly modeling reliability when incorporating predictive memory into online video systems.
icml-2026-memory-as-dynamics-learning-re.tldr: RPM regulates predictive video memory according to reliability, reducing post-occlusion drift and improving tracking and segmentation results.

paragraphs: Answering questions over FHIR health records requires navigating a directed graph of linked resources. An agent may need several steps of filtering, traversal, and aggregation to obtain an answer. Prior tool-augmented agents can choose the wrong resources or violate traversal constraints, so providing tools alone does not resolve the reasoning problem.

The paper frames this work as sequential decision-making over a queryable structured graph. The authors implement a multi-turn CodeAct agent and post-train it with reinforcement learning using a custom environment, harness, and tools. An LLM judge supplies rewards grounded in execution, connecting training feedback to the agent's actual interaction with the data.

On FHIR-AgentBench, the approach achieves 77% answer correctness with Qwen3-8B, compared with 50% for the prompt-based o4-mini baseline. The abstract describes the trained model as smaller and cheaper, while maintaining data-integrity constraints. Beyond this comparison, the contribution is an end-to-end post-training pipeline for improving multi-turn question answering over structured clinical records.
icml-2026-reinforcement-learning-for-too.tldr: An RL-trained CodeAct agent reaches 77% correctness on FHIR-AgentBench, compared with 50% for a prompt-based o4-mini baseline, while enforcing data-integrity constraints.

paragraphs: Token representations form a trajectory through a language model's internal space. Earlier observations of temporal straightening suggested that this trajectory becomes straighter across layers, potentially helping next-token prediction through linear extrapolation. This paper connects the geometry of recent context to a behavioral quantity: the entropy of the model's next-token distribution.

Across GPT-2 XL and Pythia-2.8B, contextual curvature correlates with next-token entropy, and the relationship develops during training. The authors then test interventions to distinguish a purely observational association from a feature that can influence behavior. Perturbations aligned with the representational trajectory reliably change entropy, while geometrically misaligned perturbations have no effect in the reported experiments.

The paper also regularizes representations toward straighter trajectories during training. This modestly lowers token-level entropy without worsening validation loss. Together, the results identify curvature as a task-aligned feature that influences predictive uncertainty in the studied models. The selective intervention results matter because the effect depends on how the representation is changed.
icml-2026-representational-curvature-mod.tldr: In two language models, contextual representation curvature relates to next-token entropy, and trajectory-aligned interventions can selectively change that uncertainty.

paragraphs: Low-bit quantization makes large language models more compact, but unusually large activation values can make the approximation difficult. Rotation-based methods address these outliers. A single rotation shared across layers can be fused into model weights for efficient inference, yet it offers limited flexibility. Separate layer-wise rotations adapt better but typically require extra computation during inference.

ReSpinQuant combines offline activation-rotation fusion with efficient residual subspace rotation to match bases. The design aims to retain the expressivity of layer-specific adaptation while avoiding the substantial online cost associated with conventional layer-wise methods. Its central contribution is a way to reconcile those two desirable properties.

Experiments cover four-bit weights and activations, denoted W4A4, and three-bit weights and activations, denoted W3A3. The authors report state-of-the-art performance, outperforming global-rotation methods and matching the accuracy of computationally expensive layer-wise alternatives with minimal overhead. The findings support more localized quantization adaptation without paying the usual inference cost of full layer-wise rotations.
icml-2026-respinquant-efficient-layer-wi.tldr: ReSpinQuant combines offline rotation fusion with residual subspace rotations to achieve layer-wise quantization accuracy with negligible inference overhead.

paragraphs: Diffusion models for manifold-supported data must add and remove noise in ways that respect the underlying geometry. Their training relies on the manifold heat kernel, which describes the diffusion process. Sampling from it and computing its derivatives are difficult because closed-form expressions are available for only a limited set of highly symmetric manifolds.

This paper approximates the heat kernel by solving the manifold heat equation with a physics-informed neural network. Starting from an explicit manifold specification, the authors choose coordinates, derive the associated heat equation and a short-time asymptotic approximation, and train a network to represent the log heat kernel.

The learned surrogate supports both forward noising through heat-kernel sampling and conditional-score evaluation for denoising score matching. The approach is demonstrated on the sphere S², the rotation group SO(3), positive-definite matrix manifolds, and permutation-quotiented point clouds. Its contribution is a general construction for obtaining the diffusion quantities needed for training when an explicit manifold description is available.
icml-2026-riemannian-diffusion-models-on.tldr: A physics-informed neural network approximates manifold heat kernels, enabling the noising and score calculations needed to train Riemannian diffusion models.

paragraphs: Different causal graphs can imply the same observational relationships, so distinguishing them requires restrictions on the causal model. This paper studies location-scale noise models, where causes determine both the central response and the scale of random variation. These models are flexible and identifiable in most cases, but prominent estimation approaches assume symmetric noise.

The authors show that those approaches lose performance when the noise is skewed. Their proposed method, SkewD, extends the usual normal-noise formulation to a skew-normal setting. It uses likelihood-based inference, combining heuristic search with expectation conditional maximization to estimate model parameters.

Allowing skewness enables the method to handle both symmetric and asymmetric noise within the proposed framework. This matters because imposing symmetry can distort the comparison between competing causal explanations when the data's variation is uneven. The paper concentrates on deciding causal direction between two variables and also demonstrates how SkewD can be extended to multivariate problems, giving a path beyond its main bivariate setting.
icml-2026-skewness-robust-causal-discove.tldr: SkewD extends location-scale causal discovery to skew-normal noise, addressing performance losses caused by assuming symmetric variation.

paragraphs: Vision-language models can recognize new categories without task-specific training, yet adversarial perturbations can still disrupt their predictions. Test-time defenses often adapt using many augmented versions of an image. Those extra views can improve robustness, but processing them creates a substantial speed cost and makes the quality of each view important.

SS-TPT evaluates views using two complementary signals. Stability measures whether predictions remain consistent under weak augmentations. Suitability measures how densely a view's features sit among the features of other views. These scores guide a consistency loss during prompt adaptation and determine how predictions are weighted at inference.

The method therefore uses view quality both to update the prompts and to combine the resulting predictions, emphasizing trustworthy views while reducing the influence of corrupted ones. Across diverse datasets and different numbers of views, the authors report significant improvements over prior state-of-the-art methods and a better robustness-throughput tradeoff. The results support quality-aware use of augmented views as a practical test-time defense.
icml-2026-ss-tpt-stability-and-suitabili.tldr: SS-TPT scores augmented image views for stability and suitability, improving adversarial robustness relative to inference throughput in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: Evaluating open-ended language-model answers is difficult when no ground-truth answer is available. Measures based on final-answer correctness or surface statistics also leave the construction of an argument largely unexamined. TRACE addresses that gap by evaluating the structure of a model's chain-of-thought reasoning.

The metric combines Toulmin's argumentation theory with Flavell's metacognitive framework. It examines how reasoning is assembled, providing a structural assessment that complements evaluation of the final answer. This makes the reasoning process itself an explicit object of measurement, rather than relying entirely on whether its eventual conclusion matches a reference.

Across 26.3 thousand question-answering samples and seven reasoning models, TRACE has a reported correlation of 0.74 with benchmark accuracy. Used as a reinforcement-learning reward, it also outperforms accuracy-only baselines. Together, these findings support the usefulness of structured reasoning assessment for both evaluation and training. The paper presents TRACE as a complementary metric for open-ended outputs, with evidence connecting its judgments to answer quality.
icml-2026-trace-toulmin-based-reasoning-.tldr: TRACE evaluates the structure of LLM reasoning, correlates with answer accuracy, and improves training results when used as a reinforcement-learning reward.

paragraphs: Expected information gain measures how informative a proposed experiment is expected to be. Computing it, or its derivative for optimization, can require difficult nested calculations. This paper identifies a sufficient condition under which that doubly intractable calculation can be reduced to a singly intractable expression.

The condition concerns posteriors in an exponential family whose dependence on the experimental design and observed data occurs only through their natural parameters. Under this condition, the authors derive unbiased estimators for expected information gain and its reparameterized gradient. They also show how a likelihood with an analogous form and an arbitrary prior can achieve the stated reduction.

The analysis additionally examines certain degenerate behaviors that can occur when optimizing information gain in exponential-family experiment models. Empirical comparisons show faster convergence and substantial gains in sequential design relative to standard nested estimators. The contribution is both a structural criterion for simplifying the computation and estimators that make that simplification useful for experimental design.
icml-2026-tractable-expected-information.tldr: A sufficient exponential-family condition simplifies expected information gain and its gradient, enabling unbiased estimators with improved empirical convergence.

paragraphs: Efficient attention mechanisms such as grouped-query attention and multi-head latent attention use specialized factorizations to reduce resource requirements. However, their relationship to conventional low-rank approximation can be unclear: it is not always obvious which weight objects are approximated or what ranks the resulting representations actually achieve.

This paper develops a generalized view of attention-layer weights and a corresponding factorization strategy called Tucker Attention. The framework includes ordinary multi-head attention, grouped-query attention, and multi-head latent attention as special cases. This common formulation makes it possible to analyze their achieved ranks and derive simplifications for multi-head latent attention.

In language-model and vision-transformer test cases, Tucker Attention uses an order of magnitude fewer parameters than grouped-query and multi-head latent attention while achieving comparable validation metrics. It is also compatible with flash-attention and rotary position embeddings. The contribution combines a parameter-efficient attention design with a mathematical framework for interpreting several existing architectures through the same factorization perspective.
icml-2026-tucker-attention-a-generalizat.tldr: Tucker Attention unifies several attention architectures and achieves comparable validation metrics with roughly tenfold fewer parameters in the reported test cases.

paragraphs: Reasoning systems often combine inexpensive checks, such as self-consistency or proxy rewards, with more costly external inspection. Cheap checks are scalable but imperfect, while strong verification consumes more resources. This paper studies how a system should decide whether to accept an answer, reject it, or defer to stronger verification.

The authors formalize policies that make these choices and introduce measures for incorrect acceptance, incorrect rejection, and strong-verification frequency. At the population level, optimal policies have a two-threshold structure. The analysis also identifies calibration and sharpness as properties governing how useful a weak verifier can be.

An online algorithm builds on this framework and provably controls acceptance and rejection errors without assumptions on the query stream, language model, or weak verifier. In mathematical reasoning and sequential decision-making experiments, it achieves reliability comparable to checking everything with strong verification while substantially reducing verification cost. The results support selective escalation as a way to make verification more economical while retaining error control.
icml-2026-when-to-trust-the-cheap-check-.tldr: A weak–strong verification policy decides when cheap checks suffice and when to escalate, controlling errors while reducing verification cost in experiments.
